description: A storytelling website that gives young space enthusiasts a home for the machines humanity left behind—the rovers, probes, and satellites that finished their missions but never really left us. Designed in NASA's visual language, 404: Not Found on Earth turns "gone" into "remembered."
summary:
404: Not Found on Earth is a storytelling website about Opportunity, the Mars rover humanity left behind. Designed for ages 8–15 in NASA's visual language, it tells Opportunity's story in the rover's own voice — from its 26-bounce landing in 2004, through the "blueberry" discoveries that proved Mars was once wet, to its final message in 2018. The site has three pages: Home, Opportunity, and Resources.

It addresses the challenge by turning mission data into a first-person narrative, introducing school-age audiences to the hardware left on Mars and the science it made possible. It matters because Opportunity was built for 90 days and worked for almost 15 years — and its story deserves to be remembered.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

404: Not Found on Earth is a published, three-page storytelling website about Opportunity, the Mars rover humanity left behind. The Home page introduces the concept — a 404 error means "not found" and sets the tone.

The Opportunity page tells its story as a first-person diary in four sections: its last message ("My battery is low and it is getting dark"), its 26-bounce landing in Eagle Crater, the "blueberry" discoveries that proved Mars was once wet, its adventures (the 2005 sand trap, Victoria Crater, the 2014 memory reset, the 2016 dust devil), and its final silence in 2018. Below the diary, three sections — How it was, How it is, Why it matters — anchor the story in the challenge's structure.

The Resources page credits the NASA images and mission record used. The site is navigable, responsive, and works on desktop and mobile.

What benefits does it have?

It gives school-age space enthusiasts (ages 8–15) an emotional entry point into a machine they've likely never heard of. Instead of a fact sheet, they get a story told in Opportunity's own voice — which makes the science stick. It also serves educators and casual space fans as a short, accurate, visually engaging introduction to Mars exploration and the hardware we left behind.

What is the intended impact?

To make young readers feel a personal connection to the machines we've left on other planets — and to reframe "abandoned" as "completed its work." The title carries the message: a 404 means "not found on Earth" these machines are no longer on Earth, they're retired in space, waiting to be remembered. If a 10-year-old finishes the page and feels something for a robot that stopped talking in 2018, the project has done its job.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Canva — for designing and publishing the website (layout, typography, visual system, live publishing)
  • NASA images (from the official website)
  • NASA open resources — as the factual source for Opportunity's timeline, discoveries, and final transmission
  • AI tools — used for research assistance and language polishing only(DeepSeek & Gemini); all narrative structure and creative decisions are my own, and final writing is checked strictly against the facts we collected from the NASA resources

How is your project creative?

It uses first-person perspective — the rover narrates its own story — which is rare in educational space content and instantly creates emotional connection. The diary format (dated entries) turns a mission timeline into a life story. And the visual design borrows NASA's own language — dark backgrounds, real imagery, clean type — so it feels like an official archive built for kids rather than a fan page.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: ages 8–15 — language kept short, vivid, and free of jargon
  • Accuracy: every fact drawn from NASA records; image sources credited on the Resources page
  • Accessibility: a website needs no download, works on any device, and is reachable by a single link
  • Scope: simi-Solo project, limited time — one machine told deeply rather than several told thinly
  • Tone: emotional but honest — the story ends with loss, but frames it as legacy, not failure
  • Compliance: all work completed during the hackathon; AI used only for research and polishing, and disclosed
